title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every \(n,s\ge 1\), every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and all accuracy and confidence parameters \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n,s,1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log (1/\delta )\)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
definitions: A literal is a variable \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form \((\mathrm{DNF})\) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers \(t,b\ge 2\) and set \(\varepsilon =1/t\) and \(\delta =2^{- b}\). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(p(n,s,t,b)\) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair \((x,f(x))\) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least \(1- \delta\) over the examples and internal randomness, \(\Pr_{x\text{ drawn from }D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\). Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most \(3^{n}\) simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by \((3^{n}+1)^{s}\). The finite-class union bound therefore gives \(O((ns+\log (1/\delta ))/\varepsilon )\) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical \(n^{O(s)}\) algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound \(2^{\widetilde{O} (n^{1/3} \log  s)}\). For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most \(2^{k}\) terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.

importance.reason: A defining computational learning problem originating with the PAC framework, explicitly highlighted in successive surveys and connected to representation-independent learning hardness, decision-tree learning and junta learning. Selected for the Learning theory focus prefix after correcting the mislabelled junta record; the score reflects breadth and foundational significance, not the date of this review.

progress.text: Feldman separates the general PAC question from Fourier-based learning under uniform or product distributions in the inherited source.
Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz prove improper-learning hardness under a random K-SAT refutation assumption.
Daniely–Vardi derive hardness for a growing number of DNF terms under a local-pseudorandom-generator assumption.
Servedio’s survey retains polynomial-time DNF learning as a longstanding goal and records the subexponential general upper bound.
Iterative Chow Filtering gives a quasipolynomial uniform-distribution result in a different learning model.

sentences: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of Boolean literals, representing a union of rule-defined regions.

The question asks whether an unknown DNF with at most s terms can be learned from independent labelled examples under every input distribution in time polynomial in n, s, inverse error and log inverse failure probability.
The learner may output any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis but cannot request labels for inputs of its choice.
Polynomially many samples suffice information-theoretically, while known hardness for unrestricted hypotheses relies on explicit complexity assumptions.
A solution would settle a foundational computational-learning barrier and would also yield an efficient learner for uniform-example juntas.
